To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) mt genome rearrangements have occurred independently in the two Orders, (2) mt genome organization in the most scleracatinian-like corallimorpharia, Corallimorphis profundus, resembles the common scleracatinia pattern more than that of other corallomorpharians, (3) mt genome organization is highly conserved within the Scleracatinia, (4) mt genome organization within the Corallimorphia is highly variable

the mt genome in the deep-water corallimorph Corallimorphis profundus, which is the most sclercatinian-like of all extant corallimorphs on the basis of its morphological features, shows a much greater resemblance to that of scleractinians than to the mt genomes of other corallomorpharians.

(1) the mt genome organization in the deep-water species C. profundus is much more similar to that in scleractinians than in the shallow-water species, (2) the mt genome of the deep-water species is more similar in organization to that in sclercatinians than in other corallimporpharians, and (3) the mt genomes in corallimorphians are highly rearranged relative to those in scleractinia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary relationships between corals and corallimorphs, and the potential impacts of ocean warming and acidification on the future of coral reefs.
the evolutionary relationships between corallimorphs and scleractinians and how these relationships may be used to predict the fate of coral reef ecosystems under climate change.
the evolutionary relationships between the corals and their skeleton-less sister group, the corallimorphs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mt genome organization of corallimorharians is highly variable and that this variation has important phylogenetic implications.
mt genome organization is highly labile, even in a clade of animals that is considered to be morphologically highly conservative.
the mt genomes of corallimopharians are highly variable and that the mt genome data do not support the naked coral hypothesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

mt genomes in the Hexacorallian complex (Scleratinia, Corallimorphia, Actiniaria, Zoantharia, Antipatharia, and Ceriantipatharia) are highly variable and that mt genome organization may provide an important source of phylogenetic signal in this group.
mt genome organization provides a strong signal for coral <-> corallomorpharian relationships.

the mt genome of C. profundus is a mosaic of scleractinial and corallimorphian features, and the mt genome of Corallimorphs is a mosaic of corallimopharian and non-corallimorpharian (scleractinian, zoanthids, and anemones) features.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mt genomes are not useful for understanding the relationships among the major clades within the Scleracitinia/Corallimporpharia complex.
, despite the apparent simplicity of the mt genomes of corallimorpha, mt genome organization in this group is more complicated than previously appreciated.
mt genome organization is a powerful tool for understanding coral phylogeny, but the patterns are complex and not easily interpretable.
